News COP31 delivers important progress across negotiations and Action Agenda, advancing implementation, but fails to agree Presidency-Led Decision Back COP31 delivers important progress across negotiations and Action Agenda, advancing implementation, but fails to agree Presidency-Led Decision 23 November 2026 Article Share the article Copied! --> Credit: Kiara Worth, UN Climate Change Credit: Kiara Worth, UN Climate Change --> --> UN Climate Change News, Antalya, Türkiye, 23 November 2026 – COP31 concluded with important agreements in key negotiations items, such as on a Just Transition, and concrete real-economy progress across the Global Climate Action Agenda, including a major boost for electrification. Almost 200 nations represented at COP31 also reached agreements on a range of important mandated items, relating to climate finance, adaptation, mitigation, technology, transparency and the second global stocktake, among other issues. COP31 also delivered significant new investments, and proof-points of previous initiatives being delivered, across all six Axes of the Action Agenda. The 2026 GCA Yearbook has also been updated to capture progress during the COP. Across these two parallel and complimentary tracks of the UN Climate Conferences (COPs) – negotiations and the Action Agenda – the progress achieved at COP31 will help strengthen the foundations of implementation. This is vital to help convert pledges and targets into more real-world outcomes, with more benefits for more people. However, Parties did not reach agreement on the Presidency-Led “Cover Decision” announced at pre-COP in October by the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye and the President of COP31 Negotiations of Australia, with flow-on impacts across a range of important issues and other mandated negotiations items. “I share the deep disappointment of many that COP31 has been unable to agree on issues related to the Presidency-Led Decision. There are lessons that must be learnt. Our process must follow the science and meet the challenge,” UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said, at the conclusion of COP31. “At this COP, key negotiating decisions have been made including on a Just Transition. Fairness and inclusion in the climate fight is essential. We must also recognise that this COP process has two tracks. And across the Action Agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.” “Over many COPs climate cooperation has delivered vast progress – taking humanity off an unsurvivable path of global heating. But clearly much, much more is needed. The fight continues. We will never give up,” Stiell said. Just transition Just transition is an enabler and catalyzer of climate action, ensuring faster and fairer progress with people at the centre. Under the mandated negotiations items, COP31 reviewed the United Arab Emirates just transition work programme (UAE JTWP), agreeing to continue its work for an additional three years with strengthened modalities. COP31 also recognized key messages from dialogues held under the JTWP this year, which focused on just transition in the context of food security, agriculture, oceans, industry, innovation and equitable value chains. Parties also decided to operationalize the just transition mechanism, which COP30 decided to develop last year in Belém, in a phased approach. The mechanism aims to enhance international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity building and knowledge sharing, and enable equitable, inclusive just transitions and adoption is expected at COP32. Climate finance COP31 moved climate finance from goals towards delivery. Parties took the Climate Finance Work Programme forward, renewing efforts to scale up adaptation finance, including through the transition of the Adaptation Fund to exclusively serve the Paris Agreement, and to make access to climate finance faster and more efficient. Work also continued on the wider shift in financial flows towards climate-resilient, low-emission development. Ultimately, this is about getting finance where it is needed, so countries and communities can build resilience, create economic opportunities, improve livelihoods and deliver better outcomes for people. Technology The technologies we need to tackle the climate crisis already exist. What matters now is making sure they reach the countries and communities that need them most. In Antalya, the international community took further steps to turn the promises of the Paris Agreement into action on the ground: strengthening support for countries to access and deploy climate technologies, taking forward the Belém Technology Implementation Programme, and bringing technology and finance closer together so that solutions can be implemented at scale. Adaptation COP31 advanced the operationalization of the 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators by creating a channel for countries to share experience, challenges, gaps and needs arising from voluntary country testing, and establishing a dedicated task force to improve indicator methodologies and metadata. It also reinforced implementation of the Baku Adaptation Road Map (2026–2028), initiated preparations for reviewing the UAE Framework for Global Climate Resilience, and strengthened the information base for the second Global Stocktake. Together, these steps aim to move adaptation from agreeing on global targets towards measuring collective progress, identifying gaps and accelerating implementation, while respecting national circumstances and avoiding additional reporting burdens. Decisions on the Warsaw International Mechanism and Santiago Network strengthen the focus on delivering technical assistance for loss and damage, including faster responses to requests, simplified access for vulnerable communities and arrangements to ensure that a minimum share of directly funded assistance reaches them. This is important for moving from institutional expansion to measurable support on the ground. Parties advanced work on adaptation communications, encouraging greater consistency across national adaptation plans, NDCs and transparency reports while preserving flexibility and avoiding unnecessary reporting burdens. This should help countries communicate their adaptation priorities and progress more effectively and strengthen the information base for international cooperation. Second global stocktake The second global stocktake (GST 2) – a core mechanism of the Paris Agreement – launched at COP31. The global stocktake assesses the collective progress of Parties. Its outcomes are intended to inform Parties as they strengthen their climate actions and support, on a nationally determined basis, and to improve international cooperation. GST2 will follow a three-stage process: Information collection and preparation Technical assessment, and Consideration of outputs. The process will conclude at COP 33 in November 2028, where Parties will consider the findings of the technical assessment and seek agreement on the GST2 outcome. Transparency Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) are a vital enabling tool for all governments, as well as real-economy implementers, providing a stronger evidence base for climate policy-making and engagement in climate multilateralism. BTRs play a critical role in the global stocktake (GST) process because they enable Parties to engage in the technical assessment and political consideration, grounded in the data and information owned by Parties themselves. Mandated negotiations items at COP31 agreed on underscoring that support to developing countries is crucial to sustain reporting from one cycle to the next, Parties reviewed the progress and impact of the implementation of the list of activities agreed in Belem (CMA 7) aimed towards identifying challenges in reporting faced by developing countries and possible solutions addressing the identified challenges. The review resulted in a set of guidance aimed towards further increasing the impact of the activities in 2027 and 2028. The COP31 Presidency-led ministerial high-level dialogue showed a high level of political buy-in, with Ministers and other high-level representatives reiterating the importance of climate transparency. Building on the momentum from the first cycle, many countries reaffirmed their commitment to submit their second BTRs by the 31 December 2026 deadline. Electrification surge & other progress across the Global Climate Action Agenda In parallel with the negotiated aspects of COP31, concrete real-world progress was delivered across the six axes of the Global Climate Action Agenda. Axis 1: Energy, Industry and Transport In June this year, the COP31 Presidency of Türkiye, with the support of the COP31 Presidency of Negotiations of Australia and UN Climate Change, announced a goal of 35% electrification by 2035, as a key element of the Global Climate Action Agenda. At COP31, countries representing around half of the global economy pledged their support for the 35x35 target, or their intention to achieve it earlier. “The momentum behind electrification is already strong, with more & more countries introducing new policies this year, and it is set to accelerate further thanks to the 35-by-35 Pledge. The world has entered the Age of Electricity…” said IEA Executive Director Dr Fatih Birol on LinkedIn following the conclusion of COP31. Implementation of the electrification Pledge and commitments can raise the global electrification rate from 23% to over 33% by 2035, new analysis from the International Energy Agency (IEA) shows – and could go higher if more countries join the Pledge. The IEA’s special report on Electrification published in September finds that reaching the 35% electrification rate globally has the potential to reduce emissions by at least 8 gigatonnes, even if transitions in the power mix move slowly. If they move faster, the emissions reductions could be significantly larger. Involving 150 countries from small island states to the world’s largest economies, 37 cities and more than 260 businesses with over $4 trillion annual revenue, the COP31 Electrification Delivery Package will deliver billions in clean energy investment, expand electricity access and electrify grids, transport, buildings and industry. Lessons for COP32 Addressing the closing plenary, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell acknowledged the frustration of delegates after governments failed to bridge divisions on the summit's main political decisions. “ The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment ,” he said, urging countries to learn lessons from Antalya. Mr. Stiell nevertheless highlighted progress made during the conference, including an agreement on a just transition and a series of initiatives under the COP31 Action Agenda aimed at accelerating electrification, resilience and investment. Noting that the climate process had weathered setbacks before, he said COP32 must build on previous achievements rather than “step back”. Facebook Twitter Print Email COP31 ends without climate pact as UN chief warns there is ‘no ambiguity in the science’ Conference coverage 22 November 2026 Climate and Environment COP31 ended on Sunday without a climate pact after negotiators failed to overcome divisions over fossil fuels, bringing two weeks of talks and two days of overtime to a close that UN Secretary-General António Guterres described as a “deeply disappointing” setback. Reacting to the collapse of COP31 , the Secretary-General said he was “deeply disappointed” that governments meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, had failed to reach consensus, but stressed that the outcome did not alter the realities of the climate crisis. What you need to know COP31 closed without a final climate pact after two weeks of negotiations and two days of overtime talks. Disagreement over fossil fuel language proved the main obstacle to consensus. Several countries formally objected to the final text, saying it weakened previous commitments and failed to meet the urgency of the climate crisis. António Guterres called the outcome a setback but insisted there remains “no ambiguity in the science” and urged faster climate action. Antalya has become the longest-running UN climate summit on record. ‘No ambiguity in the science’ “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science,” the UN chief said in a statement . Tweet URL He warned that global temperatures continue to break records, climate impacts are intensifying and greenhouse gas emissions remain dangerously high, while the world is now on course to exceed the internationally agreed 1.5°C warming limit. “The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis – and it must do it now,” he said. Mr. Guterres argued that fossil fuels remain the primary driver of global warming and cautioned against efforts to delay the transition to cleaner energy. “We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it,” he said, accusing powerful fossil fuel interests of obstructing climate action while continuing to profit. The Secretary-General noted that governments had already agreed at COP28 in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels and said the priority now must be to accelerate and finance that shift. He also called for deeper emissions cuts this decade, stronger support for vulnerable countries and substantially increased adaptation finance, stressing that those least responsible for climate change should not be left to bear its heaviest consequences alone. Looking beyond the negotiating halls, Mr. Guterres said the real measure of progress would be whether countries reduce fossil fuel dependence, expand clean energy, cut methane emissions, restore forests and deliver climate finance to developing nations. Addressing civil society, young people, Indigenous Peoples, scientists and frontline communities, he urged campaigners to keep pressing for action and accountability. “The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground. Neither can we,” he said. “Keep spreading the facts. Keep demanding action. Keep turning up the heat.” Days of deadlock COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, acknowledged the impasse, saying: “I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted.” The inconclusive talks followed days of deadlock over fossil fuels, with negotiators unable to bridge differences between a coalition of climate-vulnerable nations and countries pushing for a stronger commitment to move away from coal, oil and gas, and those seeking to protect economies heavily dependent on fossil fuel exports. Multiple compromise drafts circulated by COP31 co-presidents Australia and Türkiye sought to win consensus, including by acknowledging that global warming is now on course to exceed the 1.5°C threshold while calling for expanded carbon-removal technologies. But the effort ultimately failed, with critics arguing the text weakened previous commitments and fell far short of the action required to address the climate crisis. Focus now shifts to COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, where governments will face many of the questions left unanswered in Antalya, from the transition away from fossil fuels to mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. UN Climate Change/Kiara Worth; Delegations in the main hall at the closing pleanry of COP31, the latest UN climate conference, being held this year in Antalya, Türkiye. The European Union formally objected to the cover decision, saying it failed to “meet the moment” and warning that it risked widening the gap between climate commitments and real-world action. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . A crowded roadbridge near the COP31 entrance in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. (See: Cover decision .) Membership Support award-winning climate journalism Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning. With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history. Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .) While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. around: planet. While attention is diverted by geopolitical turbulence — including the Iran war, which has caused the world’s largest energy supply shock — the climate crisis is accelerating. A sobering recent UN report confirmed the world will overshoot its target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. On current policies temperatures are expected to rise to a potentially catastrophic 2.8 degrees. The planet is currently at around 1.4 degrees of warming and the impacts have been starkly clear, from catastrophic flooding in Nepal to deadly heat in Europe. Yet, COP31 laid bare the enormous gap between those seeking ambitious action, often the most climate-vulnerable countries, and the oil-rich nations pushing back. In common with previous COPs, the biggest sticking point came down to two words: fossil fuels. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to an unprecedented call to “transition away from fossil fuels.” Since then, this has neither been repeated nor built upon as oil-producing nations balk at any reference to the driving force of the climate crisis. Now there’s a plan to protect them 5 min read The first draft of the COP31 “cover decision” — which sets out the overarching agreement from the conference — was published Monday and called for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” But all mentions of fossil fuels were stripped out of every subsequent draft, despite a push by more than 100 countries to keep them in. “You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don’t need to phase out fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, COP negotiations veteran and founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. Britain’s lead climate negotiator Kate Hughes said the proposed agreement “moves us backwards,” describing it as “a lowest common denominator, where it should have been instead presenting bold, collective ambition on climate action.” Meanwhile, Amnesty International’s Climate Justice policy adviser, Ann Harrison, said countries were “right to reject” what she called a

finance. Poorer, climate-vulnerable countries have long called for more money to help them adapt to climate disasters they disproportionately face and yet did little to cause. Many developing countries expressed deep disappointment that the draft agreement called for effort to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 but included no baseline and no specific numbers. “Rich countries refused to put money on the table to help communities prepare for and recover from climate disasters, and handed polluters a free pass instead,” Singh said. “No deal is better than a deal that locks in failure.” COP31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, said the result was very disappointing but there were “a lot of good things” to come out of the talks, including more than 90 countries signing a pledge to ramp up the electrification of their economies. “What happens now is that… will continue in our renewable transition and reconvene in Ethiopia next year and see if we can’t make forward progress,” he said. Still, many experts expressed bitter disappointment at the world’s failure to meet the urgency of the climate crisis. “Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership,” said Mary Robinson, the former president of Ireland and a COP veteran. Follow The COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed Sunday as countries failed to agree to an overarching deal after more than two weeks of contentious negotiations. The breaking point was over the very cause of climate change itself: fossil fuels. The annual UN climate talks, which stretched deep into overtime over the weekend, hold the dubious honor of being the longest COP in history and the first major breakdown since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009. Experts criticized the conference as a stunning failure of leadership at a time when the climate crisis is accelerating with increasingly deadly consequences. “This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the energy think tank Power Shift Africa. Khalil Hamra/AP How two words could derail the world’s biggest climate conference 4 min read At the final meeting intended to approve the so-called Antalya Pact on Sunday, it became clear there would not be the necessary consensus between the more than 190 countries at the talks to adopt the deal. These did not include the US, which, under President Donald Trump, has pulled out of international climate action. Deep divisions proved impossible to bridge over key issues — most importantly, including language that the world would need to move away from fossil fuels, a phrase that did not end up in the agreement, and increasing financial support for countries already grappling with climate catastrophes. Petrostates, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, have long opposed the inclusion of any reference to fossil fuels. The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that rejected it. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s climate minister who is helping lead negotiations for the EU, said the bloc would not endorse a deal “that does not even mention fossil fuels.” “This COP, I believe, was hijacked by some oil states,” he later told Reuters news agency. Methane and super pollutants remain the fastest climate win Rapidly reducing emissions of methane and other short-lived climate pollutants, like black carbon, remains one of the fastest and most effective ways to slow warming during this decade, while delivering immediate benefits for health, air quality and food security. At COP31, governments and partners announced more than US$480 million to support efforts to reduce emissions of methane and other super pollutants. They also highlighted progress in strengthening methane monitoring and mitigation efforts across major emitting sectors, like oil and gas. “Reducing methane emissions is like pulling an emergency brake on climate change,” Krause said. “It can significantly slow global warming.” Governments also launched a new pledge to curb emissions of sulphur hexafluoride, the most potent greenhouse gas used to insulate electrical cables, ensuring it does not undermine the clean energy transition. 4. Extreme heat and sustainable cooling were high on the agenda Extreme heat emerged as one of the defining climate risks discussed at COP31. Governments backed the Global Heat Resilience and Sustainable Cooling Roadmap , recognizing that countries must both adapt to rising temperatures and avoid increasing emissions from the growing demand for cooling. With nearly 2 billion people lacking access to adequate cooling, the issue is increasingly being recognized as a development, health and climate priority. From energy-efficient and flexible cooling solutions to smarter buildings and nature-based solutions like planting trees, sustainable cooling offers one of the clearest examples of how adaptation and mitigation can be advanced together. 5. Better buildings and waste management gain momentum Some of the most significant progress at COP31 came from sectors that are often overlooked in climate discussions: buildings and waste. Forty-six countries backed Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings , an initiative which aims to accelerate energy efficiency improvements, renovation and electrification across the building sector. The conference also placed greater attention on waste prevention and circular economy approaches. The COP31 Presidency's Zero Waste initiative highlighted the growing role that waste reduction can play in cutting emissions, conserving resources and improving public health. Food waste reduction also gained prominence, reflecting increasing recognition of the links between waste, methane emissions, food security and sustainable development. 6. From ambition to implementation: the rise of the three roadmaps Attention increasingly centered on how to maintain momentum and deliver on three roadmaps led by the COP30 Presidency: Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, Halting and Reversing Deforestation and Forest Degradation , and mobilizing the finance needed to support both via the Baku to Belém roadmap . While disagreements remained over how to advance these roadmaps, governments, businesses and financial institutions increasingly focused on practical pathways capable of translating climate goals into real-world outcomes. During the negotiations, UNEP’s experts highlighted the importance of managing trade-offs across sectors , including ensuring that the clean energy transition can accelerate without creating additional pressure on forests. 7. Climate finance remains a major sticking point Despite progress in several areas, climate finance remained among the most contentious issues at COP31. Several countries renewed calls to significantly increase adaptation finance and improve access to funding for developing nations facing growing climate impacts. Discussions also focused on implementing previous finance commitments and identifying new funding sources. UNEP estimates that developing countries will require hundreds of billions of dollars annually to adapt to climate change by 2035, far exceeding current money flows. “We must prepare for a warmer world and reaching an agreement on climate finance is key,” Krause said. “Helping vulnerable communities adapt to a changing climate is one of the defining challenges of our time and it should bring the world together.” 8. The Global Stocktake and the Periodic Review mark a new chapter COP31 marked the formal launch of the second Global Stocktake, a process that will assess collective progress towards the goals of the Paris Agreement and help shape climate action through the remainder of the decade. The stocktake comes alongside the Periodic Review, another key scientific and political process examining the long-term climate goals and helping answer some of the most important questions facing the international community. Those include: Are countries moving fast enough? What additional action is needed? And how can ambition be translated into measurable results? Civil society: ‘A failure of political leadership’ Civil society members demonstrate at the opening of the closing plenary of COP31 in Antalya Friday. The session was later suspended until Saturday morning due to sharp disputes over a watered-down draft text. Civil society organizations were quick to denounce the summit’s failure. “This has been the worst COP ever,” lamented Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa , a Nairobi-based pan-African climate and energy think tank supporting the continent’s energy transition and climate adaptation. The World Resources Institute echoed these sentiments, blaming the results on “a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement.” Other groups vented their frustration, telling media that the conference yielded nothing that protects people — and is even a license to keep polluting. ndlessly warming world,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell warned health ministers on the conference’s opening day. The science of climate change itself was contested as ministers sought to weaken the agreement text. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told leaders the aim was to cut emissions “regardless of their sources,” despite the fact that nearly 90% of CO2 comes from fossil fuels — and pressed for later IPCC reports. The oil-rich nation insisted it was “not seeking to delay climate science.” The White House, absent for a second year, put forth an even stronger denouncement of COP31, calling the summit “climate nonsense .” Ten years from Paris a rocky road to pinning fossil fuels UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres meets with climate scientists on the sidelines of COP31. The secretary-general said that even though COP31 was without a consensus, the science is clear. The 2015 Paris Agreement never mentioned fossil fuels, although the consensus agreement to keep warming below 1.5°C was a landmark, recognizing a clear target for climate mitigation against which member states could commit through "Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and the UNFCCC could benchmark progress. Dubai in 2023 finally agreed to the language on a "transition" away from fossil fuels, and COP 30 in Belém in 2025 led to a 2026 meeting on a roadmap for doing so, launched just before COP31. And now, Antalya would not repeat even the Dubai agreement language, ultimately agreeing to nothing. Countries that want to move faster will now work through the Santa Marta process , and Panama’s call for majority voting will be harder to dismiss. In Antalya, governments were asked to say in one document that the 1.5°C limit is being breached and that coal, oil and gas are the reason. They managed the first half of that sentence. ANTALYA – After a record 44 hours of overtime, the UN climate talks in Antalya ended on Sunday night without any high-level decision document at all for the first time since the 2000 COP6 summit in The Hague. A last-ditch effort to bridge the divide between petrostates that had insisted on removing all references to fossil fuels from the initial decision draft that had been tabled earlier last week, and other nations keen to see a clear reference to the leading cause of global warming was rejected by the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Norway and small island states including Tuvalu. Countries were enraged that the compromise proposed by the co-presidencies Türkiye and Australia did not even refer clearly to the landmark agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai on "transition away from fossil fuels", making only a vague reference to the "United Arab Emirates (UAE) Consensus." Speaking for the EU presidency, Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien told the plenary : “We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels.” Conceding defeat at the closing plenary on Sunday, COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s Environment Minister, said, “I understand that there is no agreement on this text,” and then declared that the proposed Antalya Pact and its cover decision had not been adopted. He ruled out another attempt at compromise , and blamed "some" unnamed countries for failing "to demonstrate the level of commitment and flexibility required.” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “ deeply disappointed ,” warning that every delay makes the task harder and more costly, with the overshoot of the 1.5º C warming target set in the Paris Agreement in 2015 now a looming reality. “Science tells us an overshoot above that level is now inevitable,” Guterres warned in a statement, adding that ultimately, fossil fuels “ must go the way of the dinosaurs .” COP31 also became the longest UN climate conference ever , overtaking COP25 in Madrid in 2019. COP6 in The Hague failed to adopt any declaration, while COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 "took note" of that year’s cover decision, without formally adopting it — also failing to fulfil the high hopes for any real breakthrough on climate action. That breakthrough moment finally came six years later in 2015 with the Paris Agreement. Unresolved items from COP31 will now carry over automatically, under rule 16 of the UNFCCC rules of procedure, to COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027. Delegates react with disappointment The delegate from Timor-Leste, representing the least developed nations, expressed his "deep disappointment." “We have been let down on all sides,” the Marshall Islands representative told the room, while Vanuatu objected forcefully to the silence on fossil fuels, the leading cause of warming and sea level rise that is threatening the very existence of many Pacific island nations. The UK’s lead negotiator, Kate Hughes, called the text “a lowest common denominator,” while Norway said it took the world backwards from earlier agreements. Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s Minister of Environment, said on Friday said that the COP had been "hijacked by petroleum," and reminded the hall that the world was heading for 4°C before Paris, but it is on course to reach 2.8°C today. COP31 has been ‘hijacked’ by petroleum Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s Environment Minister. The third and final failed text, issued early Sunday morning, had attempted to bridge the gap between petrostates and ‘high ambition’ countries by "recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety across mitigation, adaptation and means of implementation" in its second paragraph. But the oblique reference was seen as too little, too late, by its critics, while a group of Saudi-led states as well as Russia, said they could not accept any wording on fossil fuels at all, even if based on past agreements. Saudi Arabia and other leading fossil fuel producers had argued for a text that emphasized carbon capture and storage strategies to halt runaway warming solutions that critics say are expensive and unproven at scale. Beyond that clause, health appears in four of the draft’s other 143 paragraphs, each time linked to another issue: as a benefit of climate action, in early warning systems, in human rights language, and in services for children. Negotiations in Antalya are due to close on Friday, and, in a tradition duly respected by every COP since 2003 , are likely to run overtime. The decision text and health’s inclusion in it will be up for debate until the final gavel, and many paragraphs are likely to be pruned as countries draw red lines. The COP31 presidency said in a note accompanying the draft that the text is “not intended to reflect consensus”. Every element remains open, Türkiye and Australia said, “including whether they should be included at all”. "Nothing will come out of the negotiations except for a vaguely worded statement," a Swedish observer to the negotiations told Health Policy Watch, adding: "The parties are just too entrenched in their opposing positions." Co-benefits across the text The flagship item of COP31 host Turkiye’s summit agenda has the potential to generate significant health co-benefits, but faces steep opposition. Elsewhere, the draft includes proposals with large potential health gains not directly framed as health measures. The text calls on countries to help raise electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, a headline target of Türkiye’s voluntary Action Agenda. Electrifying transport, industry and buildings would cut the fuel burning behind much of the world’s air pollution, which kills around 8 million people every year. Despite its status as the flagship initiative of the Turkish presidency, it faces steep opposition to inclusion in the final decision. The Arab Group has opposed top-down targets for energy and other sectors in the talks, and the African Group has rejected electrification targets that come without money to meet them, according to the Earth

lion this year, according to the UN Development Programme. The WHO’s own economic case for climate action rests heavily on cutting those subsidies, a Health Policy Watch analysis found. In a report released days before the summit, WHO estimated that six climate policies could prevent 1.6 million deaths a year, yet some 1.2 million of those depend on removing fossil fuel subsidies and raising taxes on coal, oil and gas. The draft addresses only “inefficient” subsidies, and says nothing about taxing fossil fuels. More health references, but few hooks for action References to health in the draft COP31 decision. Health advocates were still heartened by the increased references to health in the climate text compared to previous years. However, they stressed that this was only a first step in light of the millions of lives impacted by the "global health emergency" caused by the climate crisis that many in the health world are calling on WHO to declare. "Basically my impression is that there’s a lot of health coverage included in the current draft of the cover text but no hook for health to be more prominent in future negotiations or decisions to be implemented by countries," said WHO’s Elena Villalobos, who leads ATACH , a strategic alliance to support health sector responses to climate change. "The most important issue is related to commitments by parties to consider public health implications of all their adaptation and mitigation policies and programs although all parties to the UN Climate Convention already agreed to these commitments, and they still are not being implemented nor reported. So we need a mechanism for that," she added. See related story: Call for New WHO Instrument to Address Climate-Driven Global Health Emergency New health initiatives launched at COP31 draw few pledges and less finance Health initiatives launched at UN Climate Conferences since 2021. The potential for a breakthrough inclusion in COP31’s final decision threatens to be overshadowed by the minimal support that has accompanied other health-related initiatives in Antalya. The Antalya Initiative for Resilient Health Systems, the flagship presidency health initiative launched by Türkiye with the World Health Organization (WHO) at the summit’s opening Health Day, has yet to announce any participating countries, staff or funding. No government pledged new money for climate and health that day, the third consecutive COP without fresh government financing for health. A second new pledge, a political declaration on a “healthy transition” led by Spain, had six signatories as of Tuesday out of nearly 200 countries at the talks: Spain, France, Peru, Tuvalu, Ireland and Barbados. The declaration names fossil fuels as the main driver of climate change’s threat to health and as the cause of “millions of preventable deaths”. It co

ohol”. “The best clinical practice is one that integrates environmental perspectives in clinical decisions,” said Javier Padilla, Spain’s secretary of state for health, who spearheaded the declaration. “Putting the focus on the energy transition from the health perspective is an intelligent way to approach climate change.” The declaration, and its minimal uptake, is the kind of outcome WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned at the outset of the summit would not be enough. Declarations “do not protect people,” Tedros told health ministers gathered in a sparse conference room on COP31’s Health Day on the opening day of the conference, 9 November. “Implementation does.” See related story: ‘Declarations Do Not Protect People’: COP31 Opens Under Pressure to Deliver Results Over Words Building momentum A declaration on Climate and Health at COP28 in Dubai drew the most signatories of any, with 148 countries, but little follow-up in subsequent years. Nothing agreed or announced in Antalya so far pays for that implementation. The movement on health at COP31 builds on a patchwork of voluntary frameworks and initiatives launched alongside the UN climate talks since Glasgow, with varying levels of support. The most concrete is WHO’s Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH), launched at Glasgow in 2021, whose 106 member countries commit to building climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems. The COP28 Declaration on Climate and Health in Dubai, a broad statement of intent, drew the most signatures of any, with 148 countries. COP29 in Baku produced a coalition of five past and incoming summit presidencies pledging to keep health on the COP programme, outside the formal negotiations. The Belém Health Action Plan, the most detailed of all, has 40 signatories so far, up from 33 when it was announced at the close of COP30 last year. Implementation absent from mounting pile of plans Top health and climate officials gather at a high-level ministerial meeting on COP31’s Health Day. But while declarations and initiatives have launched, the money to act on them has yet to follow. In a WHO survey last year, more than 90% of countries named insufficient finance as a top barrier to their health and climate plans, Tedros said in his Health Day comments. Multilateral climate funds have directed about 2% of adaptation finance and 0.5% of all their climate finance to health since 2004, according to a 2025 analysis by the Berlin-based think tank adelphi, roughly the share WHO reported at Glasgow. The Green Climate Fund, the UN’s largest climate fund, had financed a single health project in Malawi, as of COP29. On Health Day, Brazil’s health minister Alexandre Padilha said international public commitments for health adaptation fell from about $3.2 billion in 2022 to $2.2 billion in 2024. He also launched a “financing framework” for the Belém plan, develope

in its first year and attracted $150 million in new commitments. “There’s no way that philanthropy can fill the hole or deliver health systems for whole countries,” said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome, a coalition member. “Governments are slow-moving beasts and sometimes require a bit of a nudge.” “The first thing we can do is provide some technical advice to give you some ideas of what needs to change,” he said. “Then of course finance needs to follow. That is a huge problem.” No country asked to put health on the agenda Delegates gather for the opening ceremony of COP31 in Antalya. No country pressed to have health on the formal negotiating agenda of this year’s conference. While health may at least get more of a mention in the final text, no country asked to add health to the formal negotiating agenda in Antalya. “[Health] belongs in the negotiated text,” Tedros told ministers on Health Day. “It should be an explicit eligibility area for climate finance and its share should grow as adaptation finance grows.” Only governments can propose items for the negotiating agenda, and they must file before a session opens. None of the agendas for COP31, the parallel Paris Agreement meeting or the two technical bodies that prepare their work lists a health item, indicating no country pursued the idea despite WHO’s vocal push. With the COP31 agenda adopted on 9 November, the earliest health could gain an item of its own is the June 2027 technical sessions in Bonn or COP32 in Addis Ababa. A government would need to file in time, and no country could object when the agenda is adopted. While WHO has argued for a dedicated negotiating track, other civil society groups with which Health Policy Watch spoke in Antalya expressed a preference for health to run through existing negotiations, warning that a standalone item could paradoxically cut health out of higher-profile parts of the talks. One way or another, however, the endgame is the same: more investments in health-related climate action by countries and international actors.
